title: How boiling, steaming, microwaving and stir-frying change the vitamin C in vegetables

facts.text: Vitamin C dissolves in water; the body cannot make it or store it, so it must come from food regularly.
The body needs vitamin C to make collagen, heal wounds, keep bones and teeth healthy and absorb iron.
Too little vitamin C can cause bleeding gums, easy bruising and slow wound healing; the severe form is called scurvy.
Raw fruits and vegetables are the best sources; cooking or long storage can lower their vitamin C.
Vitamin C breaks down easily with heat, and high temperatures and long cooking times cause especially large losses.
A Korean study (published 2018) cooked ten vegetables by blanching, boiling, steaming and microwaving and measured their vitamins.
The study reported true retention, which compares the total vitamin in the cooked food with that in the raw food, allowing for changes in weight.
Across all cooked samples in that study, vitamin C retention ranged from 0 to about 91 percent.
In that study, boiling generally gave the lowest vitamin C retention and microwaving the highest.
Vitamin C retention (%) after boiling, steaming and microwaving: spinach 40.12, 44.75, 91.10; potato 49.79, 83.65, 76.86.
Vitamin C retention (%) after boiling, steaming and microwaving: sweet potato 73.86, 59.44, 100.21; carrot 55.33, 70.51, 92.02.
Vitamin C retention (%) after boiling, steaming and microwaving: zucchini 63.71, 89.24, 92.73.
In chard, both boiling and steaming left no measurable vitamin C, while microwaving kept 67.64 percent.
Steaming and microwaving kept more vitamin C than boiling because the food touches less water.
The authors advise using little cooking water and short cooking times to keep more vitamin C.
A Chinese study (2009) compared steaming, microwaving, boiling, stir-frying and stir-frying followed by boiling for broccoli.
In the broccoli study, steaming caused no significant loss of vitamin C; every other method caused a significant loss.
In the broccoli study, boiling lost 33 percent of vitamin C and stir-frying then boiling lost 38 percent, more than stir-frying alone.
In the broccoli study, stir-frying alone lost less vitamin C than boiling but still lost much more than steaming.
The broccoli study says the vitamin is lost mainly by leaking into the surrounding water when broccoli is boiled.
The researchers note stir-frying is among the most popular home cooking methods in China and suggest steaming broccoli instead.
Derived from the table values: boiling gave the lowest retention for four of the five vegetables (all but sweet potato), and microwaving the highest for four (all but potato).

notes: 批次規格建議「幾種蔬菜用水煮、蒸、炒之後維生素 C 保留的比例」；Our World in Data、World Bank、data.gov.tw 都沒有烹調方式與維生素保留率的資料集，也找不到同一研究同時量測多種蔬菜水煮、蒸、炒的公開數據，所以表格改用最接近的真實資料：Lee et al. 2018 Table 2（多種蔬菜的水煮、清蒸、微波；期刊資料只取事實，數字寫在 f10–f12，沒有 datasets）。快炒的比較取自 Yuan et al. 2009 的青花菜研究（f16–f20）：該文結果段寫快炒損失 24%、討論段寫 16%，前後不一，所以事實單只記錄「快炒損失少於水煮、多於清蒸」這類兩段一致的結論，不寫快炒的百分比。
